assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the trade-shock evidence changed how economists and policymakers understand labour demand, wage inequality and the local costs of adjustment. It combines a clear explanatory framework with new empirical designs, which fits the standard of data discovery plus an explanatory framework. The policy and societal impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to the task framework and the China-shock work. Katz is central to the earlier supply-and-demand framework for wage structure. Hanson is a core co-author on the trade-shock design. Dorn is also a key co-author on the China-shock papers and is omitted only because of the three-name limit, which makes the attribution contestable. Katz also appears on B017.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly 1992 to 2020 and has had decades of replication, extension and debate. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer the task framework or the trade-shock design as the core, and so which three to name.
Dorn's omission and Katz's multiple credits complicate attribution.
Some China-shock magnitudes and long-run interpretations are still contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks are a foundational mechanism in macro-finance. The framework was reinforced by the 2008 crisis and now underlies much policy analysis. It has deep theoretical and applied influence.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clear originators of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler is central to the financial accelerator and its quantitative integration into DSGE models. Gilchrist is an important empirical contributor but less central. Bernanke's earlier prize for banks and crises overlaps in theme, and Gertler also appears on B049.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and has long been validated through the financial crisis and a large follow-on literature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises could weigh against the field.
The three-name split depends on how the financial accelerator is credited relative to the collateral-constraint papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Demand estimation with differentiated products and dynamic industry models became the standard toolkit for empirical industrial organisation. It is used widely in antitrust, merger review and regulation, so it has real methodological and practical impact.
assessment.attribution: Pakes and Berry are the dominant figures, through BLP and the dynamic and estimation methods. Levinsohn is a co-author of BLP. Bresnahan, who is also credited, is arguably as important for the empirical IO agenda and could replace Levinsohn. The list is crowded, so the choice is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 1994 to 1995 and has been used for decades, so recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan or Levinsohn should be named alongside Pakes and Berry.
This is a methodological contribution, and committees differ on how they weigh toolkits against discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reorganised international trade theory and the measurement of gains from trade. They moved the field from sector-level to firm-level analysis and connected well to micro data. The influence on later work is very large.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the origin of the heterogeneous-firm trade model. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, developed the model's extensions and firm-level evidence. Redding is a major later contributor but a more junior figure on this specific advance. Helpman is also credited on B021.
assessment.maturity: The work is over two decades old and mainstream, with extensive empirical confirmation.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize on new trade theory partly overlaps in theme.
It is unclear whether Redding should be added, and how the credit divides between Melitz and Helpman.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work built a modern political economics that links constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity to fiscal outcomes. It has both a theoretical framework and empirical tests, and it has influenced the study of institutions and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures, through their work on constitutional and electoral rules and public policy. Besley is closely tied on state capacity and political agency. Credit is spread across many co-authors and subtopics.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from the 1990s to the 2000s and has been extended, tested and applied across many settings.
uncertainties: The relation to the institutions prize of 2024 may reduce the novelty of the field.
Causal evidence on some cross-country findings is mixed, and the credit is diffuse.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The use of population administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects created new facts and a new empirical agenda. It has had large social and policy influence and is very close to my own use of administrative data.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the programme. Hendren and Friedman are central co-authors on mobility and neighbourhood effects. Katz is credited here but is already better placed on B013.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from about 2014 to the present. Several findings are still being replicated or debated, and the long-run causal interpretation is unsettled, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Debate over the causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects and the stability of the mobility estimates.
Chetty's very broad portfolio also appears on B015, so it is unclear which contribution would be recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance work opened a large empirical literature linking legal institutions and investor protection to financial development, and it links finance with institutions and law. Its influence on the field is large.
assessment.attribution: Shleifer is the leading figure and La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes are the principal co-authors. Vishny shares in the earlier corporate-governance papers. A three-name limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are from 1997 to 2008. They are very influential but have been challenged on the legal-origins thesis, so the evidence is mixed.
uncertainties: Legal-origins identification and measurement of the anti-director index have drawn serious criticism.
Shleifer's broader work spans many topics, so the prize motivation is ambiguous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Empirical measurement of taxable-income responses and its link to optimal-tax theory (the sufficient-statistics approach) had substantial influence on public finance and policy. It joins theory to evidence and the policy relevance is high.
assessment.attribution: Saez and Slemrod are the strongest credits on the taxable-income elasticity agenda. Chetty's sufficient-statistics work is an important link. Stantcheva is promising but more recent. Saez and Chetty also appear on other candidates.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s to the 2010s and is well established, although estimates of the elasticity vary across settings.
uncertainties: Estimates of the elasticity of taxable income are sensitive to the design and time horizon.
Saez and Chetty are credited on several candidates, so it is unclear which contribution would be recognised.
